processing: A pan-fired flat green tea made in the Longjing manner: as with other Longjing-style teas, the leaf is fixed and pressed flat in a hot wok, with no oxidation.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual picking for Longjing-style greens, with the earliest lots prized; local picking dates for Bikou are not well recorded.
appearance_dry: Tender green, even and clean, in the flat shape typical of Longjing-style tea.
appearance_wet: As with other Longjing-style teas, soft tender buds and young leaves of a fresh yellow-green.
taste_profile: Rich chestnut aroma over a mellow, full and clean-sweet cup.

brewing.notes: Usual treatment for a flat green tea: a glass or open gaiwan, water well off the boil, and leaf left uncovered so it does not stew.

vintage_note: Like other green teas of its kind, it is bought as the current spring harvest and is best drunk within the year. Longjing from outside Zhejiang is a separate product from the protected West Lake and Zhejiang names, so the label should state Gansu or Bikou plainly.
description:
This is Longjing from an unexpected place: the Bikou area of Wenxian county in Longnan, in the far south of Gansu. The Longnan counties of Wen, Wu and Kang are among the northernmost tea land in China, which makes this one of the more curious relatives of the Hangzhou original.

The method and the name come from Zhejiang, and the look follows: flat leaf in a tender, even green. Treat it as a Longjing-style tea, not as an imitation of West Lake; the place is different and so is what you should expect.

The cup is described as apricot green with a strong chestnut aroma and a mellow, sweet finish. Brew it like other flat greens, with cooler water and an open vessel.

It is mostly a regional tea, and Bifeng Longjing is the name you may also see. Ask for the harvest date and for Wenxian or Bikou on the pack, since the word Longjing alone tells you very little.
history:
Longjing began around West Lake in Hangzhou. Green tea in the Longjing style has been grown successfully in Wenxian since the late 1950s, and it is now counted among the better-known Longjing areas outside Zhejiang.

One account gives Bikou town five tea bases, 23,710 mu of tea gardens and about 239 tonnes a year. These figures have no date attached, so treat them as a rough picture of scale.
